title: Ἔχις καὶ ὕδρος
part: The Viper and the Water-snake (Chambry 117 · Perry 90)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 117 (= Perry 90). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔχις φοιτῶν ἐπί τινα κρήνην ἔπινεν.
sentences.tr: Echis phoitōn epi tina krēnēn epinen.
sentences.l: A viper, resorting to a certain spring, used to drink.
sentences.i: A viper used to come to a certain spring and drink there.
sentences.n: φοιτάω is to go somewhere regularly, back and forth; with the imperfect ἔπινεν it makes the drinking a settled habit, which is what gives the water-snake his grievance.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐνταῦθα οἰκῶν ὕδρος ἐκώλυεν αὐτόν, ἀγανακτῶν ὅτι μὴ ἀρκεῖται τῇ ἰδίᾳ νομῇ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ δίαιταν ἀφικνεῖται.
sentences.tr: Ho de entautha oikōn hydros ekōlyen auton, aganaktōn hoti mē arkeitai tēi idiāi nomēi, alla kai epi tēn autou diaitan aphikneitai.
sentences.l: But the water-snake living there tried to prevent him, being indignant that he was not content with his own pasture, but came also to the other's dwelling.
sentences.n: ἐκώλυεν is a conative imperfect — he tried to stop him, without succeeding. The ὅτι-clause is negated by μή rather than the οὐ classical prose would use here; it puts the grievance as the water-snake sees it rather than as a flat statement of fact. ἴδιος ('his own') is set against αὐτοῦ ('the other's'), which is the whole quarrel: stay in your own range.

sentences.t: Ἀεὶ δὲ τῆς φιλονεικίας αὐξανομένης, συνέθεντο ὅπως εἰς μάχην ἀλλήλοις καταστῶσι καὶ τοῦ νικῶντος ἥ τε τοῦ ὕδατος καὶ τῆς γῆς νομὴ γίνηται.
sentences.tr: Aei de tēs philoneikias auxanomenēs, synethento hopōs eis machēn allēlois katastōsi kai tou nikōntos hē te tou hydatos kai tēs gēs nomē ginētai.
sentences.l: And the rivalry ever increasing, they agreed that they should enter into battle with one another and that the pasture both of the water and of the land should be the winner's.
sentences.i: As the rivalry kept growing, they agreed to join battle with each other, and that the grazing of both water and land should belong to the victor.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, this one with ἀεί: 'the quarrel growing all the while'. ὅπως with the subjunctive after a verb of agreeing gives the terms agreed on. τοῦ νικῶντος is a predicate genitive of possession — the pasture is to 'be the winner's'; the present participle leaves the winner unnamed, whoever he turns out to be.

sentences.t: Ταξαμένων δὲ αὐτῶν προθεσμίαν, οἱ βάτραχοι διὰ μῖσος τοῦ ὕδρου παραγενόμενοι πρὸς τὸν ἔχιν παρεθάρσυνον αὐτόν, ἐπαγγελλόμενοι καὶ αὐτοὶ συμμαχήσειν αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Taxamenōn de autōn prothesmian, hoi batrachoi dia misos tou hydrou paragenomenoi pros ton echin paretharsynon auton, epangellomenoi kai autoi symmachēsein autōi.
sentences.l: And they having appointed a set day, the frogs, out of hatred of the water-snake, having come to the viper, kept encouraging him, promising that they too would fight as his allies.
sentences.i: When they had fixed the day, the frogs, who hated the water-snake, came to the viper and kept heartening him, promising that they too would join the fight on his side.
sentences.n: προθεσμία is the appointed term, the day named in advance and binding on both parties. συμμαχήσειν is a future infinitive — after verbs of promising Greek looks forward with the future, where English says 'promised to fight'. The frogs' hatred is a genitive of the object hated: μῖσος τοῦ ὕδρου.

sentences.t: Ἐνστάσης δὲ τῆς μάχης, ὁ μὲν ἔχις πρὸς τὸν ὕδρον ἐπολέμει, οἱ δὲ βάτραχοι μηδὲν περαιτέρω δρᾶν δυνάμενοι μεγάλα ἐκεκράγεισαν.
sentences.tr: Enstasēs de tēs machēs, ho men echis pros ton hydron epolemei, hoi de batrachoi mēden peraiterō dran dynamenoi megala ekekrageisan.
sentences.l: And the battle having set in, the viper on his side was fighting against the water-snake, while the frogs, being able to do nothing further, were crying loudly.
sentences.i: When the battle was joined, the viper fought the water-snake, while the frogs, able to do nothing more, set up a loud croaking.
sentences.n: ἐκεκράγεισαν is a pluperfect doing the work of an imperfect: κράζω forms a perfect κέκραγα with present force, 'I am in full cry', so its pluperfect simply means 'they were in full cry'. The verb is used of the harsh noise of birds and frogs. μεγάλα is adverbial accusative, 'greatly, loudly'.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ ἔχις νικήσας ᾐτιᾶτο αὐτοὺς ὅτι γε συμμαχήσειν αὐτῷ ὑποσχόμενοι παρὰ τὴν μάχην οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐβοήθουν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ᾖδον.
sentences.tr: Kai ho echis nikēsas ēitiato autous hoti ge symmachēsein autōi hyposchomenoi para tēn machēn ou monon ouk eboēthoun, alla kai ēidon.
sentences.l: And the viper, having won, blamed them because, having promised to fight as his allies, throughout the battle they not only did not help but even sang.
sentences.i: And the viper, when he had won, reproached them: they had promised to be his allies, and all through the battle they not only gave no help but actually sang.
sentences.n: παρά with the accusative of time means 'all through, during'. οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί is the standard 'not only … but even', and the sting is in the last word: ᾖδον, 'they sang', a mocking name for the croaking of the previous sentence.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἔφασαν πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’ εὖ γε ἴσθι, ὦ οὗτος, ὅτι ἡ ἡμετέρα συμμαχία οὐ διὰ χειρῶν, διὰ δέ μόνης φωνῆς συνέστηκεν. »
sentences.tr: Hoi de ephasan pros auton· « All’ eu ge isthi, ō houtos, hoti hē hēmetera symmachia ou dia cheirōn, dia de monēs phōnēs synestēken. »
sentences.l: But they said to him: « Nay, know it well, you there, that our alliance consists not of hands but of voice alone. »
sentences.n: ὦ οὗτος is a hail rather than a courtesy — 'you there', brisk and a little rude. συνέστηκεν, perfect of συνίστημι, is 'has been put together, consists in'. διὰ χειρῶν stands for action that costs something; the frogs concede the point without embarrassment.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι, ἔνθα χειρῶν χρεία ἐστίν, ἡ διὰ λόγων βοήθεια οὐδὲν λυσιτελεῖ.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti, entha cheirōn chreia estin, hē dia logōn boētheia ouden lysitelei.
sentences.l: The story shows that, where there is need of hands, the help that comes by way of words is of no use at all.
sentences.n: χρεία takes the genitive of the thing needed. ἡ διὰ λόγων βοήθεια packs the prepositional phrase between article and noun — a favourite Greek move, and the reason the literal line needs a relative clause in English.
